common_name: Golden Anniversary Baptisia (Golden-Foliage Indigo-Blue False Indigo)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun, choosing a permanent site since Baptisia develops a deep taproot and resents transplanting once established; Golden Anniversary is a Walters Gardens introduction notable for combining indigo-blue flowers with golden-yellow foliage.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun, choosing a permanent site since the deep taproot resents transplanting once established. Golden Anniversary is the first widely available Baptisia to pair true indigo-blue flower spikes with foliage that emerges and holds a striking golden-yellow color through the growing season, giving the compact, ball-shaped plant a two-toned effect unlike any older cultivar. Flower spikes rise just above the foliage in late spring to early summer, followed by dark ornamental seedpods that persist into fall, and both the flowers and colorful foliage are useful in cut arrangements. Like other Baptisia it is extremely drought-tolerant, deer-resistant, and essentially maintenance-free once established, needing only an occasional late-winter cutback and no routine division.

common_name: Decadence Deluxe Honey Roasted Baptisia (Bicolor Dark Yellow and Burgundy-Brown False Indigo)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun, choosing a permanent site since Baptisia develops a deep taproot and resents transplanting once established; Honey Roasted is a Hans Hansen introduction in the Decadence Deluxe series bred for unusually warm bicolor flower tones.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun, choosing a permanent site since the deep taproot resents transplanting once established. Honey Roasted bears bicolor flower spikes about 10 inches long in dark yellow and warm burgundy-brown, with the flowers lightening toward yellow as they age so a single spike shows a warm, toasted gradient found in no older Baptisia cultivar. As a Decadence Deluxe selection it grows larger than the original Decadence series, forming a substantial, shrub-like clump, and its flowers are followed by ornamental black seedpods that add fall and winter interest. Established plants are extremely drought-tolerant and essentially pest-free, needing no division and improving in flower production for many years.

common_name: Indigo Spires Baptisia (Deep Violet-Purple False Indigo Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun to light partial shade, choosing a permanent site since Baptisia develops a deep taproot and resents transplanting once established; Indigo Spires is a Baptisia australis x Baptisia alba hybrid grown for its exceptionally long flower spikes.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun to light partial shade, choosing a permanent site since the deep taproot resents being moved once established. Indigo Spires produces exceptionally long, 12- to 15-inch flower spikes of deep violet-purple, pea-like blossoms accented by a yellow keel, borne on all sides of a bushy, upright, blue-green-leaved clump, and secondary spikes continue to open after the main flush, extending bloom into midsummer. Following flowering, dark seedpods provide fall and winter interest, and the deep violet-blue flowers are a favorite of bumblebees and other pollinators. It is extremely drought-tolerant and essentially maintenance-free once established, functioning like a small flowering shrub; avoid dividing or transplanting mature plants, and simply cut back in late winter if a tidier form is wanted.

common_name: Callilepsis Liatris (Tall Dark Cut-Flower Gayfeather Selection)

planting.note: Plant corms 3 to 4 inches deep in well-drained, average to poor soil in full sun in spring; Callilepsis is a vegetatively propagated selection of Liatris spicata grown commercially for its taller, darker, more uniform flower spikes.

directions: Plant corms 3 to 4 inches deep, flat side down, in well-drained, average to poor soil in full sun in spring; rich or wet soil produces floppy growth. Callilepsis was selected from Liatris spicata for taller, darker purple, and more uniformly shaped flower spikes than the straight species, opening from the top of the spike downward and holding color for a week or more once cut, which has made it a mainstay of commercial cut-flower production. Its strong, straight stems and dense, richly colored spikes stand out in the summer border as well as in bouquets, and the fuzzy purple flowers are highly attractive to bees and butterflies. Divide congested clumps of corms every three to four years in spring to maintain vigorous flowering.

common_name: Trailblazer Liatris (Compact Sun-Tolerant Blue-Green-Leaved Blazing Star)

planting.note: Plant corms 3 to 4 inches deep in well-drained, average soil in full sun in spring; Trailblazer is a tetraploid Liatris spicata selection with fine, bluish-green foliage that resists wilting better than older cultivars such as Kobold.

directions: Plant corms 3 to 4 inches deep, flat side down, in well-drained, average soil in full sun in spring. Trailblazer is a tetraploid improvement on the older Kobold cultivar, staying compact at 24 inches or a bit taller while offering fine, bluish-green leaves that hold up noticeably better in hot, sunny conditions without the midday wilting seen in some other blazing star selections. Thick spikes of purple flowers open from the top downward in summer and gradually turn black as they go to seed, providing food for finches if left standing, while the plant's dense, non-flopping habit suits the front to middle of a sunny border. It is a strong pollinator and butterfly plant that tolerates heat and drought once established; divide congested clumps of corms every three to four years in spring to keep them vigorous.
